definition: Lithe means flexible and graceful in movement — a body that bends and flows with ease.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word lithe. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know lithe should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Otters are lithe enough to turn a full circle inside their own length.
Limber means loose enough to move and stretch — it stops well short of lithe.
Supple goes further than limber — it bends softly, without resistance — but stops short of lithe, which adds grace to the bending.

Nimble is about speed and lightness — quick feet, quick fingers, quick wits. Lithe is about how the body bends: flexibility carried with grace, the flowing ease of a dancer or a cat. A nimble mover darts; a lithe mover flows.

Agile is athletic quickness — changing direction fast, in control, like a point guard. Lithe cares less about speed than about grace: a body that bends and flows softly through a motion. An agile mover is quick and sure; a lithe one is supple and beautiful to watch.

Old English lithe left no everyday descendants — its one child, the fairy-tale word lithesome, is rarer than lithe itself. The root's whole career in modern English is this single supple adjective.
Lithe means flexible and graceful in movement — a body that bends and flows with ease.
In the tango final, the oldest couple on the floor won on lithe economy: no lunges, no strain, just long supple turns that seemed to have no corners at all.
Lithe says more than 'flexible' — it bundles bend and grace into one word.
A gymnast's stretched hamstring is flexibility; movement that flows soft and effortless through every joint is lithe, and the word always compliments.
Lithe is for living bodies in motion — dancers, cats, willows — and it always admires.
Choose supple when you mean pure soft bendability, nimble when you mean quickness, and lithe when flexibility moves with grace.
It rarely fits objects or ideas: a lithe argument sounds as odd as a graceful doorknob.

Most of the climbing gym's regulars muscle their way up the wall, all grip strength and lunges.
Mara does something different.
Coaches call her style lithe: she pours herself from hold to hold, hips and shoulders bending in one continuous line.
Watching from below, you rarely see a sudden move.
The route seems to unroll at whatever slow speed she chooses.
A visiting coach once filmed her and slowed the tape further, expecting to find hidden bursts of effort.
Frame by frame, the climb was a single unhurried curve from floor to ceiling.
